claim: The chromatophore of purple bacteria is an intracellular spherical vesicle that exists in numerous copies in the cell.
source: The chromatophore of purple bacteria is an intracellular spherical vesicle that exists in numerous copies in the cell and that efficiently converts sunlight into ATP synthesis, operating typically under low light conditions.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the chromatophore structure and abundance.

claim: The chromatophore efficiently converts sunlight into ATP synthesis.
source: The chromatophore of purple bacteria is an intracellular spherical vesicle that exists in numerous copies in the cell and that efficiently converts sunlight into ATP synthesis, operating typically under low light conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a functional characteristic of the chromatophore.

claim: The chromatophore operates typically under low light conditions.
source: The chromatophore of purple bacteria is an intracellular spherical vesicle that exists in numerous copies in the cell and that efficiently converts sunlight into ATP synthesis, operating typically under low light conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characteristic of chromatophore operation.

claim: Quinol turnover at the cytochrome bc1 complex is rate limiting in the chromatophore.
source: The steady-state ATP production rate as a function of incident light intensity is determined after identifying quinol turnover at the cytochrome bc1 complex (cytb⁢c1) as rate limiting and assuming that the quinone/quinol pool of about 900 molecules acts in a quasi-stationary state.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: The quinone/quinol pool of about 900 molecules acts in a quasi-stationary state.
source: The steady-state ATP production rate as a function of incident light intensity is determined after identifying quinol turnover at the cytochrome bc1 complex (cytb⁢c1) as rate limiting and assuming that the quinone/quinol pool of about 900 molecules acts in a quasi-stationary state.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption in the abstract for the model.

claim: For an illumination condition equivalent to 1% of full sunlight, the vesicle exhibits an ATP production rate of 82 ATP molecules/s.
source: For an illumination condition equivalent to 1% of full sunlight, the vesicle exhibits an ATP production rate of 82 ATP molecules/s.
evidence: This is a direct quantitative result stated in the abstract.

claim: The energy conversion efficiency of ATP synthesis at illuminations corresponding to 1%–5% of full sunlight is calculated to be 0.12–0.04, respectively.
source: The energy conversion efficiency of ATP synthesis at illuminations corresponding to 1%–5% of full sunlight is calculated to be 0.12–0.04, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct quantitative result stated in the abstract.

claim: The vesicle stoichiometry is evolutionarily adapted to the low light intensities in the habitat of purple bacteria.
source: The vesicle stoichiometry, evolutionarily adapted to the low light intensities in the habitat of purple bacteria, is suboptimal for steady-state ATP turnover for the benefit of protection against over-illumination.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The vesicle stoichiometry is suboptimal for steady-state ATP turnover for the benefit of protection against over-illumination.
source: The vesicle stoichiometry, evolutionarily adapted to the low light intensities in the habitat of purple bacteria, is suboptimal for steady-state ATP turnover for the benefit of protection against over-illumination.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding of the study.

claim: Photosynthetic organisms absorb sunlight and utilize the Förster mechanism for efficient excitation energy transfer.
source: These organisms absorb sunlight and subsequently utilize the Förster mechanism (Sener et al., 2011) and quantum coherence (Strümpfer et al., 2012; Panitchayangkoon et al., 2010; Scholes, 2010) for efficient excitation energy transfer, followed by conversion of light energy into chemical energy (Feniouk and Junge, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Photosynthetic organisms utilize quantum coherence for efficient excitation energy transfer.
source: These organisms absorb sunlight and subsequently utilize the Förster mechanism (Sener et al., 2011) and quantum coherence (Strümpfer et al., 2012; Panitchayangkoon et al., 2010; Scholes, 2010) for efficient excitation energy transfer, followed by conversion of light energy into chemical energy (Feniouk and Junge, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The light harvesting system of purple bacteria is claimed to be the earliest of the current photosynthetic lineages.
source: The light harvesting system of purple bacteria (Hu et al., 2002; Cartron et al., 2014) is claimed to be the earliest of the current photosynthetic lineages (Xiong et al., 2000) and exhibits, at the supra-molecular level as well as at the level of individual proteins, less complexity than the thylakoid membranes of the more ubiquitous cyanobacteria and plants (Kirchhoff et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The light harvesting system of purple bacteria exhibits less complexity than the thylakoid membranes of cyanobacteria and plants.
source: The light harvesting system of purple bacteria (Hu et al., 2002; Cartron et al., 2014) is claimed to be the earliest of the current photosynthetic lineages (Xiong et al., 2000) and exhibits, at the supra-molecular level as well as at the level of individual proteins, less complexity than the thylakoid membranes of the more ubiquitous cyanobacteria and plants (Kirchhoff et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In Rhodobacter sphaeroides the basic photosynthetic unit is the chromatophore.
source: In the purple bacterium Rhodobacter (Rba.) sphaeroides the basic photosynthetic unit is the chromatophore (Cogdell et al., 2006; Strümpfer et al., 2011; Cartron et al., 2014), a 50–70 nm diameter vesicle, as shown in Figure 1, formed through invagination of the intracytoplasmic membrane (Tucker et al., 2010; Gubellini et al., 2007) and comprising over a hundred protein complexes (Jackson et al., 2012; Woronowicz and Niederman, 2010; Woronowicz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The chromatophore is a 50–70 nm diameter vesicle.
source: In the purple bacterium Rhodobacter (Rba.) sphaeroides the basic photosynthetic unit is the chromatophore (Cogdell et al., 2006; Strümpfer et al., 2011; Cartron et al., 2014), a 50–70 nm diameter vesicle, as shown in Figure 1, formed through invagination of the intracytoplasmic membrane (Tucker et al., 2010; Gubellini et al., 2007) and comprising over a hundred protein complexes (Jackson et al., 2012; Woronowicz and Niederman, 2010; Woronowicz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The chromatophore is formed through invagination of the intracytoplasmic membrane.
source: In the purple bacterium Rhodobacter (Rba.) sphaeroides the basic photosynthetic unit is the chromatophore (Cogdell et al., 2006; Strümpfer et al., 2011; Cartron et al., 2014), a 50–70 nm diameter vesicle, as shown in Figure 1, formed through invagination of the intracytoplasmic membrane (Tucker et al., 2010; Gubellini et al., 2007) and comprising over a hundred protein complexes (Jackson et al., 2012; Woronowicz and Niederman, 2010; Woronowicz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The chromatophore comprises over a hundred protein complexes.
source: In the purple bacterium Rhodobacter (Rba.) sphaeroides the basic photosynthetic unit is the chromatophore (Cogdell et al., 2006; Strümpfer et al., 2011; Cartron et al., 2014), a 50–70 nm diameter vesicle, as shown in Figure 1, formed through invagination of the intracytoplasmic membrane (Tucker et al., 2010; Gubellini et al., 2007) and comprising over a hundred protein complexes (Jackson et al., 2012; Woronowicz and Niederman, 2010; Woronowicz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The proteins that constitute the chromatophore are primarily the light harvesting complexes, photosynthetic reaction centers, cytb⁢c1 complexes, and ATP synthases.
source: The proteins that constitute the chromatophore are primarily the light harvesting (LH) complexes, photosynthetic reaction centers (RCs), cytb⁢c1 complexes, and ATP synthases, which cooperate to harvest light energy for photophosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of chromatophore composition.

claim: The architecture of the chromatophore has been determined by combining atomic force microscopy, cryo-electron microscopy, crystallography, optical spectroscopy, mass spectroscopy, and proteomics data.
source: The architecture of the chromatophore, reported in (Şener et al., 2007, 2010; Cartron et al., 2014), has been determined by combining atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Bahatyrova et al., 2004; Olsen et al., 2008), cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) (Qian et al., 2005; Cartron et al., 2014), crystallography (Koepke et al., 1996; McDermott et al., 1995; Papiz et al., 2003; Jamieson et al., 2002), optical spectroscopy (Hunter et al., 1985; Sener et al., 2010), mass spectroscopy (Cartron et al., 2014), and proteomics (Jackson et al., 2012; Woronowicz and Niederman, 2010; Woronowicz et al., 2013) data.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The composition of the chromatophore depends on growth conditions such as light intensity.
source: The composition of the chromatophore depends on growth conditions such as light intensity (Adams and Hunter, 2012; Woronowicz et al., 2011b, 2011a) and can also be influenced by mutations (Siebert et al., 2004; Hsin et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The composition of the chromatophore can be influenced by mutations.
source: The composition of the chromatophore depends on growth conditions such as light intensity (Adams and Hunter, 2012; Woronowicz et al., 2011b, 2011a) and can also be influenced by mutations (Siebert et al., 2004; Hsin et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The membrane of 16,000 lipids contains the quinone/quinol pool of about 900 molecules.
source: The membrane of 16,000 lipids contains the quinone/quinol pool of about 900 molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption describing the model composition.

claim: The chromatophore displays organizational principles for the integration of multiple processes.
source: The chromatophore displays organizational principles for the integration of multiple processes (Sener et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Evolutionary competition at the organism level has driven photosynthetic subsystems toward optimal and robust function.
source: Evolutionary competition at the organism level has driven photosynthetic subsystems toward optimal and robust function (Noy et al., 2006; Noy, 2008; Scholes et al., 2011) that can guide the design of artificial light harvesting devices such as biohybrid antennas (Harris et al., 2013) and nanopatterned light harvesting (LH) complex arrays (Reynolds et al., 2007; Vasilev et al., 2014; Patole et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The quantum yield does not constitute a limiting factor for the overall energy conversion efficiency in the chromatophore.
source: Clearly, the quantum yield does not constitute a limiting factor for the overall energy conversion efficiency in the chromatophore.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the quantum yield value.

claim: At light intensities equivalent to 1% and 3% of full sunlight, the vesicle is found to produce ATP molecules at a rate of 82 s−1 and 118 s−1, respectively.
source: At light intensities equivalent to 1% and 3% of full sunlight, the vesicle is found to produce ATP molecules at a rate of 82 s−1 and 118 s−1, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct quantitative result stated in the Results section.

claim: At the high-light limit, the ATP synthesis rate approaches 158 molecules s−1.
source: At the high-light limit, the ATP synthesis rate approaches 158 molecules s−1.
evidence: This is a direct quantitative result stated in the Results section.

claim: The ATP synthesis rates are consistent with experimental observations for continuous light-induced photophosphorylation, reported to be in the range of 0.017 molecules per BChl per second and 0.05 ATP molecules per BChl per second.
source: These rates are consistent with experimental observations for continuous light-induced photophosphorylation, reported to be in the range of 0.017 molecules per BChl per second (Saphon et al., 1975) and 0.05 ATP molecules per BChl per second (Clark et al., 1983), corresponding to ~43 ATP molecules s−1 and ~130 ATP molecules s−1, respectively, for the vesicle shown in Figure 1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The energy conversion efficiency at 1% and 3% of full sunlight is 12% and 7%, respectively.
source: The corresponding energy conversion efficiency, ηA⁢T⁢P, at the stated low-light intensities of 1% and 3% of full sunlight, calculated in the present study, are 12% and 7%, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct quantitative result stated in the Results section.

claim: An upper-limit of 30% was estimated for the conversion efficiency of photosynthesis in Rba. sphaeroides.
source: Notably, an upper-limit of 30% was estimated in (Hellingwerf et al., 1993) for the conversion efficiency of photosynthesis in Rba. sphaeroides.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The efficiency value computed for the recently established model of the chromatophore ranges between 0%–17%.
source: In comparison, the efficiency value, ηA⁢T⁢P, computed for the recently established model (Cartron et al., 2014) of the chromatophore (Figure 2) ranges between 0%–17%.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The role of closed and open RCs in determining the overall efficiency of the photosynthesic apparatus had been already pointed out long before any structural details were known.
source: Remarkably, the role of closed and open RCs in determining the overall efficiency of the photosynthesic apparatus had been already pointed out long before any structural details were known (Vredenberg and Duysens, 1963).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: At peak solar intensity photovoltaic-driven electrolysis is reported to have an energy conversion efficiency of 5–15%.
source: At peak solar intensity photovoltaic-driven electrolysis is reported to have an energy conversion efficiency of 5–15% (Blankenship et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Pigment networks of individual light harvesting proteins were reported to display optimality and robustness in their quantum yield with respect to the spatial organization of pigments and the site energy distribution.
source: For instance, pigment networks of individual light harvesting proteins were reported to display optimality and robustness in their quantum yield with respect to the spatial organization of pigments and the site energy distribution (Şener et al., 2002; Noy et al., 2006; Damjanovic et al., 2002); a similar robustness was reported with respect to size-scaling deformations of an entire vesicle (Sener et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The steady state ATP synthesis is not optimized by the vesicle composition shown in Figure 1.
source: Clearly, steady state ATP synthesis is not optimized by the vesicle composition shown in Figure 1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The turnover rate would be improved by an nB:nL ratio that is greater than the native value of 1:3.
source: The turnover rate, kATP, would be improved by an nB:nL ratio that is greater than the native value of 1:3 (Crofts, 2004; Cartron et al., 2014), as suggested also by a comparison of the turnover times at cytb⁢c1 and RC (τB/τL≃8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: A single ATP synthase is sufficient to take advantage of proton turnover of an entire chromatophore.
source: A single ATP synthase is sufficient to take advantage of proton turnover of an entire chromatophore (Etzold et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Vesicles have been found to occasionally fuse through formation of membrane tubes permitting passage of protons between neighboring chromatophore vesicles.
source: In this regard, it is of interest that vesicles have been found to occasionally fuse through formation of membrane tubes (Tucker et al., 2010) permitting passage of protons between neighboring chromatophore vesicles, thereby sharing their proton gradients with the ATP synthases of multiple vesicles, reducing the need for back-up ATP synthases and even permitting less than one ATP synthase per vesicle.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The efficiency curve determined for the purple bacterial chromatophore indicates specialization for low-light intensities.
source: The efficiency curve determined in the present study for the purple bacterial chromatophore (Figure 2B) indicates specialization for low-light intensities.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The chromatophore composition appears to be suboptimal for ATP production under steady-state illumination.
source: The chromatophore composition appears to be suboptimal for ATP production under steady-state illumination.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The chromatophore is a highly specialized device that performs its energy conversion function robustly for low average light intensity, while featuring protective measures that dissipate energy at higher light intensity.
source: The chromatophore is apparently a highly specialized device that performs its energy conversion function robustly for low average light intensity, while featuring protective measures that dissipate energy at higher light intensity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary interpretation.

claim: Robustness against damage appears to supersede optimality under idealized conditions.
source: Robustness against damage, such as overacidification of the membrane due to sustained overillumination, appears to supersede optimality under idealized conditions, such as steady state illumination.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The inner diameter of the vesicle is 50 nm.
source: The inner diameter of the vesicle is 50 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption.

claim: The model is based on AFM, EM, crystallography, mass spectroscopy, proteomics, and optical spectroscopy data.
source: The model is based on AFM, EM, crystallography, mass spectroscopy, proteomics, and optical spectroscopy data (Cartron et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption with a supporting citation.

claim: At 1% of full sunlight, the ATP production rate is 82 s−1, which is 79% of the maximum possible rate among all stoichiometries.
source: The reference vesicle (Figure 1) is represented by a circle, corresponding to an ATP production rate of 82 s−1 (118 s−1), i.e. 79% (51%) of the maximum possible rate among all stoichiometries, for 1% (3%) of full sun light.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 3 caption.

claim: At 3% of full sunlight, the ATP production rate is 118 s−1, which is 51% of the maximum possible rate among all stoichiometries.
source: The reference vesicle (Figure 1) is represented by a circle, corresponding to an ATP production rate of 82 s−1 (118 s−1), i.e. 79% (51%) of the maximum possible rate among all stoichiometries, for 1% (3%) of full sun light.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 3 caption.

claim: The chromatophore model comprises 16,000 lipids and 900 quinones, corresponding to a system containing 100 million atoms, including solvent.
source: The chromatophore model shown in Figure 1 comprises, in addition to the aforementioned constituent proteins, 16,000 lipids and 900 quinones, corresponding to a system containing 100 million atoms, including solvent.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the model.

claim: This system has been equilibrated through a 100 ns MD simulation to test the viability of the model employed.
source: This system has been equilibrated through a 100 ns MD simulation to test the viability of the model employed.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the model validation.

claim: Chromatophore vesicles typically contain 1–2 ATP synthases.
source: Chromatophore vesicles typically contain 1–2 ATP synthases (Feniouk et al., 2002; Cartron et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: Proteomics studies suggest preferential co-location of ATP synthase with LH2 subunits.
source: Proteomics studies suggest preferential co-location of ATP synthase with LH2 subunits (Woronowicz and Niederman, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: The quinone/quinol pool and the proton gradient function as energy buffers between light harvesting and ATP synthesis stages.
source: The quinone/quinol as well as the generated proton-motive force function as energy buffers between light harvesting and ATP synthesis stages.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the energy conversion process.

claim: The chromatophore utilizes the generated proton motive force for NADH production via NADH dehydrogenase.
source: In addition to ATP synthesis, the chromatophore utilizes the generated proton motive force also for NADH production via NADH dehydrogenase (Klamt et al., 2008) and, thereby, for control of the quinone/quinol pool redox state.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: Efficient energy conversion requires some degree of robustness with respect to supramolecular organization, since no two chromatophores are likely to be identical.
source: Efficient energy conversion requires some degree of robustness with respect to supramolecular organization, since no two chromatophores are likely to be identical.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a general principle.

claim: Robustness in photosynthetic systems had been demonstrated computationally for the excitation transfer step of light harvesting at the single protein level with respect to loss or rearrangement of pigments.
source: Robustness in photosynthetic systems had been demonstrated computationally for the excitation transfer step of light harvesting at the single protein level with respect to loss or rearrangement of pigments (Şener et al., 2002) as well as against fluctuations of pigment site-energies (Damjanovic et al., 2002) and at the vesicle level against deformations of the pigment network (Sener et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: The quantum yield is solely a function of pigment network geometry and is independent of incident light intensity.
source: The quantum yield is solely a function of pigment network geometry, is independent of incident light intensity, and is found to be close to unity (Strümpfer et al., 2012; Sener et al., 2011) for initial chlorophyll light absorption; in case of carotenoid light absorption the quantum yield can be lower due to so-called covalent electronic excitation as argued in (Ritz et al., 2000b).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: The quantum yield is found to be close to unity for initial chlorophyll light absorption.
source: The quantum yield is solely a function of pigment network geometry, is independent of incident light intensity, and is found to be close to unity (Strümpfer et al., 2012; Sener et al., 2011) for initial chlorophyll light absorption; in case of carotenoid light absorption the quantum yield can be lower due to so-called covalent electronic excitation as argued in (Ritz et al., 2000b).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: In case of carotenoid light absorption the quantum yield can be lower due to so-called covalent electronic excitation.
source: The quantum yield is solely a function of pigment network geometry, is independent of incident light intensity, and is found to be close to unity (Strümpfer et al., 2012; Sener et al., 2011) for initial chlorophyll light absorption; in case of carotenoid light absorption the quantum yield can be lower due to so-called covalent electronic excitation as argued in (Ritz et al., 2000b).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: Carotenoids transfer excitation within less than a picosecond to a nearby BChl.
source: Carotenoids transfer excitation within less than a picosecond to a nearby BChl (Damjanović et al., 1999; Berera et al., 2009) and also play a role in quenching triplet states of BChls through reverse excitation transfer (Ritz et al., 2000a).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: Carotenoids play a role in quenching triplet states of BChls through reverse excitation transfer.
source: Carotenoids transfer excitation within less than a picosecond to a nearby BChl (Damjanović et al., 1999; Berera et al., 2009) and also play a role in quenching triplet states of BChls through reverse excitation transfer (Ritz et al., 2000a).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: Exciton-based excitation transfer in the chromatophore proceeds within 10–100 ps.
source: Exciton-based excitation transfer in the chromatophore proceeds within 10–100 ps (Sener et al., 2011), first among the LH2s, then from LH2 to LH1, and finally from LH1 to the four BChls of the RC (Visscher et al., 1989; Beekman et al., 1994; Strümpfer and Schulten, 2012a; Sener et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: Electronic excitation energy absorbed directly or indirectly by a BChl is rapidly shared between BChls within individual LH1 and LH2 light harvesting complexes, forming, within about a ps, thermally equilibrated exciton states.
source: Electronic excitation energy absorbed directly or indirectly (through carotenoids) by a BChl is rapidly shared between BChls within individual LH1 and LH2 light harvesting complexes (Cory et al., 1998), forming, within about a ps, thermally equilibrated exciton states as established experimentally (Visser et al., 1996; Jimenez et al., 1997; Valkunas et al., 2007) as well as computationally (Strümpfer and Schulten, 2009; Strümpfer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: The high quantum yield is achieved because loss due to internal conversion and fluorescence arises much more slowly (rates about (1 ns)−1) than excitation transfer or charge separation at RC (rates about (10 ps)−1).
source: Such high value for the quantum yield, close to the ideal limit of 1, is achieved because loss due to internal conversion and fluorescence arises much more slowly (rates about (1 ns)−1) than excitation transfer or charge separation at RC (rates about (10 ps)−1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for the high quantum yield.

claim: The time-scale with which the quinone/quinol pool redox state adapts to a change in light conditions is reported to be about 0.5 s.
source: The time-scale with which the quinone/quinol pool redox state adapts to a change in light conditions is reported to be about 0.5 s (Woronowicz et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The present study differs from earlier studies in functional modeling of the chromatophore in that it is based on an explicit atomic-detail structural model.
source: The present study differs from earlier studies in functional modeling of the chromatophore (Geyer et al., 2007, 2010) in several respects: first, it is based on an explicit atomic-detail structural model; second, instead of employing many (over 30) adjustable parameters, few experimentally determined rate constants are employed to describe the rate determining steps; third, a steady-state description is chosen such that energy conversion steps that are not rate-limiting can be left out of the kinetic model.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The present study employs few experimentally determined rate constants to describe the rate determining steps instead of many adjustable parameters.
source: The present study differs from earlier studies in functional modeling of the chromatophore (Geyer et al., 2007, 2010) in several respects: first, it is based on an explicit atomic-detail structural model; second, instead of employing many (over 30) adjustable parameters, few experimentally determined rate constants are employed to describe the rate determining steps; third, a steady-state description is chosen such that energy conversion steps that are not rate-limiting can be left out of the kinetic model.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Primary conclusions reached presently would not be affected by a more detailed description of individual proton translocation steps and proton motive force conversion.
source: Primary conclusions reached presently would not be affected by a more detailed description, i.e., the model is robust with respect to the neglect of explicit modeling of individual proton translocation steps and proton motive force conversion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an assessment of model robustness.

claim: Integrative models of organelle function such as the one presented here provide a bridge between experimental methods that do not resolve temporal and spatial detail needed for establishing physical mechanisms and microscopic simulations that span the multiple length and time scales relevant for the function of living cells.
source: Integrative models of organelle function such as the one presented here provide a bridge between experimental methods that do not resolve temporal and spatial detail needed for establishing physical mechanisms and microscopic simulations that span the multiple length and time scales relevant for the function of living cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a broader perspective on the study.
